articles.text: After years of community input and planning, the Linda Beach Tot Lot by Beach School will soon reopen with fresh play equipment, safer surfacing and a bright, inviting look designed for the youngest residents. The tot lot has always been more than a playground. It is where new parents meet, grandparents linger on sunny benches, and toddlers take their first wobbly steps toward the slide. Families can look forward to swings, slides and low climbing features sized for ages two to five, along with interactive panels and balance elements that encourage imagination and movement. The new rubber play surface is designed as a cheerful path for little explorers, with color blocks and gentle curves that make even a short loop feel like an adventure. Fencing and pathways will provide easier access for strollers. Neighbors helped shape the upgrade through months of outreach and surveys, with parents, caregivers and even tots weighing in on favorite features. Top requests included an enclosed layout, a welcoming theme, and classic play elements like climbing and sliding. The result is a cozy, modern take on a neighborhood playground that still feels New Linda Beach Tot Lot is coming soon

articles.text: Editor: We are writing to express our support and gratitude to the School Board and administration for their recent decision to add a new Honors English class for 10th graders at Piedmont High School. This is an important step toward addressing a long-standing equity gap between STEM and humanities course offerings at the secondary level. Piedmont students with interests and talents in STEM have had early access to advanced coursework beginning in 6th grade with compression math and continuing in 10th grade with advanced science courses. By contrast, students whose strengths lie in the humanities (reading, writing, history, and the arts) have had to wait until their junior year for comparable rigor and depth in their PHS classes. The addition of an Honors English course for 10th graders begins to correct this imbalance. We are encouraged by ongoing conversations between district administrators and teachers about adding an advanced history option, such as AP Modern World History, for 10th graders. We sincerely hope that an accelerated history course can be added for the 2026/27 school year. While we share concerns about our high school students feeling pressure to take too many advanced classes to be competitive for college admissions, the current proposal is about choice and equity - ensuring that humanities-focused students have some earlier access to advanced coursework that STEM students have long enjoyed. Thank you for your thoughtful leadership on this important issue and for your continued dedication to all of our students. articles.text: Editor: I voted for our school board members because I was excited about the policies and approaches that I believed they all would bring to the district. At the October 8th board meeting there was a rigorous and honest discussion about our curriculum at the high school level and I wanted to publicly thank the board for taking the positions that they did. Piedmont went through a period where we drifted away from rigorous academic standards and having high expectations for our kids. I am glad to see us shifting back in the other direction and I believe the last board vote was an important step in the right direction. As echoed by many of our board members — and very appropriately named by Max Roman, Ruchi Medhekar and Lindsay Thomasson — we should work hard to push against the soft bigotry of low expectations, believe that our kids can do hard things, and help them prepare for a competitive and (unfortunately) unforgiving adult world. If we don’t, they’ll be significantly disadvantaged when they get to college and when they get into the workforce. Just ask anyone who teaches college students or hires recent grads and you will hear them lament the general unpreparedness of these young adults. I also wanted to say that Ruchi’s comments at the end were some of the most thoughtful, cogent and authentic commentary that I’ve heard from a public figure (especially an unpaid, volunteer). Her point about stress and challenge growing over time is one I wholeheartedly support. We should let our kids experience manageable stress and challenge now when the stakes are significantly lower than they ever will be in their lives. I have never been more excited about the direction our district is headed. The decisions, leadership and community outreach from Dr. Hawn and Ariel Dolowich demonstrate they are a team that is seeking the best for our students, our families, and trying to make it work with our teachers. I know these positions are often difficult to take because there are so many constituents to balance in the district so a big thank you to them for taking a principled, logical and appropriate approach to our kids’ futures. Above all else I appreciate the swiftness with which they make decisions and the humility they have to understand if those decisions need to be reversed or changed. It is clear that these are not universally popular decisions. Nothing worth deciding ever is. There are a myriad of ways we can address concerns such as caps on APs or limiting the weighted grades. But denying choice is not the right solution. I stand by the board’s vote on Wednesday. Adam Fishman

articles.text: Trudy is a 7-year-old, 10-pound Chihuahua mix who is slowly warming up in her foster home. Her fosters say Trudy is the perfect foster: house-trained, cratetrained, polite with the resident animals, and happy to enjoy whatever tasty treats are offered. She’s still building trust with people, but once she’s feeling safe she’ll gently melt into arms for scritches and pets. Her fosters believe Trudy will thrive in a calm home with another small dog and a patient adopter who can let her develop at her own pace. If you’d find joy in watching a timid pup blossom into a cuddly companion, Trudy just might be the little shadow you’ve been waiting for. Follow her @foster_mutt_motel on Instagram. articles.text: Morton and Aquarius are a charming pair who balance each other beautifully. Morton, a 3-year-old tuxedo with bright green eyes and extra toes, is confident, social, and full of personality. Aquarius, a tiny, 7-month-old tortie with an inquisitive streak, adds sweetness and kitten-like charm to the mix. Morton loves chasing wand toys and pouncing on his favorite fish toy, while Aquarius prefers graceful wand play. She looks to Morton for confidence, following his lead as she warms up to new people. Once settled, she’s affectionate and playful, showing off her silly side. Both cats enjoy companionship and attention. Morton can sometimes get overstimulated with too much handling, while Aquarius may start out a little hand-shy, so they’ll do best with adopters with cat experience who can tune into their cues. articles.text: Annual ShakeOut drill is a reminder to be ready for earthquakes Pause what you are doing at 10:16 a.m. on Thursday, Oct. 16, and practice what to do during an earthquake as part of the Great California ShakeOut. Anytime you feel shaking or receive an alert, take these three steps immediately if you are able: • Drop to your hands and knees. This position helps prevent a fall and reduces the chance of being hit by falling or flying objects. • Cover under a sturdy desk or table. Stay on your knees, bend over to protect vital organs, and cover your head and neck with one arm. If no shelter is nearby, crawl next to an interior wall. • Hold on until the shaking stops. If you are under furniture, hold it with one hand and be ready to move with it if it shifts. If not, hold your head and neck with both arms and hands. If you use a wheelchair or walker: • Lock the wheels of your device. • Cover your head with your hands and arms. • Hold on until the shaking stops. Living near the Hayward Fault means earthquakes are part of our future. Learning and practicing “drop, cover, and hold on” can significantly reduce the chance of injury during the initial shaking. The Piedmont Fire Department encourages everyone to join the drill. After practicing, take a few more steps to prepare: • Sign up for AC Alert emergency notifications at acalert. org • Check and refresh your disaster supply kit • Make a plan for how you will notify loved ones of your status after an emergency International ShakeOut Day is held each year on the third Thursday of October to help communities protect themselves during earthquakes. Register at shakeout.org for tips on planning your own drill and talking with others about preparedness.

articles.text: Health Class teacher Lael McAuliffe MHS student representative to the school board Saniyah Johnson Piedmont’s School Board conducted a first reading at its meeting on October 8 concerning its plan to update Piedmont’s graduation requirements. The changes align with the University of California’s A-G requirements for UC admissions. The planned changes would eliminate the requirements for graduation of semesters of computer science, health education and ethnic studies; those classes would still be offered but would be electives. The plan would also change the math requirement from two to three years, eliminates the option for visual and performing arts to count for foreign language study and requires students to have two years of foreign language. A waiver is proposed for students unable to meet these new requirements to still graduate. “We believe that offering A-G requirement, which almost 97% of our students currently meet, raises the floor and allows our students to maximize what they are taking as they proceed through their high school career,” said Assistant Superintendent Ariel Dolowich. “I want to be abundantly clear that the purpose of this policy is to allow students to make more choices in determining what courses make sense for them. We are not taking anything away. I hear the narrative that we are eliminating Health to add APs, that is inaccurate,” said Thomasson. Public comments, limited to two minutes and 30 seconds each, were largely against the proposed changes. “I fear that students that do not choose a third year of math [will] find themselves at risk of not graduating,” said math teacher Sam Colburn. Among others, Counselor Chris Hartford and Health Science teacher Lael McAuliffe spoke about removing the requirement for students to take the Health Class. “The Health class, by nature, [helps] the most vulnerable kids who need the most. [Those students] hang out with the teacher, it’s like [the class acts] as a Wellness Center. I basically fear that without that class we are going to miss [supporting] those kids,” said Hartford. “Health is not an elective topic, it is a life skill,” said McAuliffe. “The CDC reports that nearly one in three teens experiences persistent sadness or hopelessness.” “I thought long and hard about [the Health class] as well, it really does matter, we are all deeply invested in the social emotional health of kids,” said board member Susy Struble. “Again, the class is not going away, I know that feels like small comfort.” “The second that we saw any issues with our student health and wellbeing that we could tie back to the lack of having this as a requirement at sophomore year we would change it right back,” said Struble. Ethnic Studies teacher Gabby Kashani reminded the board that she fought to get the Ethnic Studies class into PHS despite the disfavor of former Asst. Superintendent Cheryl Wozniak. Kashani recalled how once the class was offered, the board in 2020 then thanked her for bringing the class to Piedmont one year before the state mandate. “I took Ethnic Studies and I feel like it really helps broaden kid’s perspectives and outlooks on different things and cultures,” said junior Saniyah Johnson Millennium High student rep to the board. “Things are not always as it is in your own bubble and community.” For teachers and counselors speaking at the meeting, there was a definite connection between adding more AP classes, which was next on the agenda, and making room by removing requirements of health and ethnic studies. “I know and I have seen the stress of students, even now currently coming into my office, just to ask me a question, I feel like they are nervous,” said Counselor Stefanie Manalo-Leclair. “I want us to pay attention to our students mental and emotional health, if there is an increase in APs and honors, that will not be a choice, they will sign up for it.” PHS student representative to the board Hunter Fasteau also wore his heart on his sleeve, makEthnic Studies teacher Gabby Kashani ing comments with Johnson, two hours into the meeting at around 9:00 p.m. “There is an indescribable feeling of inadequacy amongst students when they cannot achieve their best,” said Fasteau. “I know in myself that I have to go home and study for 2-3 more hours for homework due tomorrow, while also dedicating time to being here, to doing something that I care about.” “We can’t lose sight that human beings have to grow and mature and develop outside of the classroom,” added Fasteau. The board did not vote on the item, as it was a first reading.

articles.text: At the October 8 School Board meeting, several new courses were approved for Piedmont High School, including AP Business with Personal Finance, AP Research, Honors English for sophomores, Honors Ceramics, and Honors Art. At the same time, Health was removed as a required course, and Ethnic Studies, another unweighted class, was no longer mandatory. While the changes were intended to broaden academic opportunities, many students worry they will increase stress and competition. Freshman Dario Banuelos voiced concern about removing Health. “I believe the removal of health as a required course was a mistake as it is one of the most applicable classes and helps greatly to stay mentally and physically healthy. Doing this while also adding a number of more stressful classes doesn’t do much except hurt the environment at PHS.” Many students said the decision felt rushed and disconnected from actual student needs. Senior Kalyani Spieckerman explained, “Parents and adults keep arguing that it’s important to have weighted humanities classes to balance out the STEM ones, but it’s harmful to have that many weighted classes at all. It will make kids feel immense pressure to take the harder option, even if it’s not right for them.” Spieckerman added that Piedmont’s culture already promotes the idea that unweighted classes are “less than,” pressuring students to take more rigorous tracks. “With more weighted classes, we’re going to see kids opting into courses they probably shouldn’t take just to avoid social consequences,” she said. Sophomore Stella Joseph argued, “I feel like introducing these classes will only put more pressure on the students to take them at a younger age or only pursue the courses with weighted options rather than pursuing something they are more interested in.” This pressure is amplified by how colleges evaluate course rigor: colleges consider the total number of APs a student could have taken, not just those they actually enroll in. If a school adds more AP options, a student who takes only a portion, say ten out of 20, may appear less ambitious, even if those ten already represent a significant challenge. As a result, students feel compelled to overload themselves, prioritizing transcript appearance over genuine learning or well-being. Sophomore Cory Minor said, “Adding more weighted classes would make Piedmont’s already super competitive atmosphere ten times more competitive.” Junior Heiko Sexton-Boer, who spoke at the meeting, expressed his frustration about how the adults went about it. “I talked with some of the board members after the meeting and was told their ultimate goal was to create weighted classes for sophomores. They met that goal, but they could’ve taken more steps and avoided all this backlash,” he said. Sexton-Boer said he was not diametrically opposed to adding more weighted classes, but suggested the issue lies more in how and why decisions were made than in the courses themselves. Not all students oppose the changes. Sophomore Lukas Bekele said, “I like that they’re adding more weighted classes that are interesting. I think Business with Personal Finance sounds great.” Freshman Danilo Titterton acknowledged both sides, “I think that the new additions of APs have benefits and downsides.” Many students argue that the focus should be on meaningful learning and emotional well-being, not just the number of weighted courses on a transcript. Parents often fail to recognize how much academic pressure has changed. Unlike a decade ago, students must balance APs, extracurriculars, leadership roles, and community service just to remain competitive for college. As colleges increasingly value balance, curiosity, and emotional health, students fear these curriculum changes push them toward burnout and away from genuine learning. Seniors, amid college applications, feel these changes entrench a culture where success is measured by grades rather than personal growth. Senior Athena Li summed up the sentiment: “I wish there was more of a way for [PHS] seniors to express our opinions, feedback, and experience. Even if we won’t be affected, we care. We’ve been here the longest, taken the most APs, seen the most changes, and truly know best what it’s like to be a student at PHS, so it’s really a disservice to the underclassmen and juniors that this experience is essentially lost.” Many students also feel powerless, as their concerns are often met with dismissal or negativity from the adults who hold decision-making power, a reality made clear when students and teachers voiced opposition to the additions, yet the changes still passed. This highlights the frustration of being constantly told to advocate while seeing the very adults in their community undermine their voices. Evolette Mak is an intern with the Piedmont Post and a senior at Piedmont High School.

articles.text: On Thursday, October 9, more than 70 donors and supporters of the Piedmont Unified School District (PUSD) Wellness Center gathered at the home of Liz and Gregor Watson for a sponsor appreciation event. This year’s Wellness Center campaign raised a record $67,200 to support the mental health of Piedmont students. The PUSD Wellness Center serves students at Piedmont High School, Piedmont Middle School and Millennium High School. It provides a familiar space on campus where trained staff connect teens to the right level of counseling support. articles.text: Have you ever seen a dog shake someone’s hand or sit on command? Believe it or not, keepers at Oakland Zoo work with our animals to train them to behave similarly. If you are at the Zoo at the right time, you might see a bear standing up with front paws on the fence, a macaw being asked to put its wing out, or other interesting behaviors from the Zoo animal residents. Our animals are trained to exhibit different behaviors to help us better care for them. For example, a bear standing up with paws on the fence allows Keepers to check their belly and feet for injuries. This helps ensure the animals are happy and healthy in a safer, more frequent, and less stressful manner. Animal Training Game Using a “bridge” signal during training helps animals understand what action is rewarded, reducing confusion. This signal, such as a whistle or clicker, bridges the gap between the desired action and the reward, which is usually a yummy treat. For this game you will “train” another person to act. First, send the person who will be the trainee into another room, so the person guiding them can decide on a task. Once the trainer chooses the action, the trainee re-enters the room, and the people guiding use claps to direct the trainee. The claps are slow at first and then speed up as the person gets closer and closer to the correct action. The clapping acts as your “bridge” guiding the person to the proper action. Nathaniel Landers is Manager of Teen Outreach at Oakland Zoo. Got a burning question for an animal expert? articles.text: Piedmont suffered a 3-0 loss to league foes Alameda, but kept the scores close. Piedmont High’s girls’ volleyball team traveled to Alameda for a Western Alameda County Conference match on Thursday, October 9, falling by a 3-0 score. Despite the sweep, the Highlanders held tight at different points in each set, losing by scores of 25-15, 25-23, and 25-23. “I give them the formula and sometimes it takes them a couple of sets to apply it. When they execute, they realize what’s going wrong early,” coach Mariah Cardenas said. The result brings Piedmont’s record to 8-8 with four matches remaining on their schedule. PHS must attain a .500 winning percentage to qualify for the North Coast Section postseason, but could still be eligible for an at-large bid. PHS has remained competitive in all of their eight losses. In fact, 13 of their total losing sets were separated by just five points or less. With eight sophomores, five juniors, and just two seniors, Piedmont has shown great potential. “I think we know what we have to do, but we make bad errors at bad times. There are some high intensity moments, and you notice some anxiety out there. This league is tough, and Staff Photos we are small from a stature standpoint. We’re really young, but we’re gaining knowledge. There are definitely growing pains,” Cardenas said. Match Recap In the first set, Alameda opened to a 7-1 lead, but Piedmont stormed back with five straight points to make it a 7-6 deficit. From there, Piedmont kept the set within a three points deficit, including a four-point run to make it 15-13 Alameda, but couldn’t pull ahead. Trailing 17-14, Alameda closed the set with eight of nine points to win 25-15. Maika Ting logged 14 kills against Alameda. Stella Wilk had six kills in the match with he Hornets.

articles.text: In a rivalry match for Piedmont High’s girls’ tennis team the Highlanders beat the Bishop O’Dowd Dragons 5-2 on Thursday, October 9 at Merritt College in Oakland. The result improves PHS’ record to 9-8 overall and 3-1 in the Western Alameda County Conference. Clinching Thursday’s match day was the No. 2 doubles team of Maddie Tran and Inara Mehta with an exciting three sets, 7-5, 3-6, 6-3. “We were warming up in the first set and then cooled off in the second. Our coaches gave us good advice after that. One of their girls kept hitting down the line, so I had to adapt to that,” Tran said. “We were down in the first set and then we came back. The second set was a little rougher than we would’ve liked. I was missing some shots and volleys, but then we pulled it all together in the third set,” Mehta added. The duo has played alongside each other all season as Piedmont’s second doubles team. It marks their first time playing together after Tran combined with Emma Chan last season at No. 2 doubles and Mehta paired with graduate Abigail Call at No. 3 doubles. Mehta won Thursday’s match with a powerful overhand at the net. “I think we’ve gotten better at setting up our points in terms of winning at the net. Maddie is really good at lobbing and that sets me up well. It’s important to set up those points and win those points,” Mehta said. “We’ve definitely gotten better working with each other, especially at the net. She angles the ball really well when I’m at the net, where the other team is forced to hit it up or to me. I’ll be able to end the point like that,” Tran said. Thursday’s victory featured freshman Ella Ruthven defeating O’Dowd’s No. 1, junior Ayla Akcaoglu, in straight sets, 6-4, 6-4. articles.text: It was a difficult way to start their Western Alameda County Conference Mission Division schedule for the Piedmont High football team, suffering a onesided 63-7 loss to the visiting Hayward Farmers at Witter Field on Friday, October 10. Piedmont held a 7-6 lead with two minutes left in the first quarter, but things began to unravel after Hayward returned the ensuing kickoff for a touchdown. “It’s 0-1, the message is its just one game and it’s not going to make or break our season. Our goals aren’t changing. We knew it would be a learning year, we’re not physical enough just yet, that’s the hump we have to get over,” said coach Jordan Seiden. It marks the Highlanders’ second consecutive sizeable defeat after falling to Arroyo 40-26 the previous week. PHS notably was without star running back and linebacker Xavier Henderson, who won our Athlete of the Month award in September. Starting offensive and defensive lineman Bill Ashton was also out, creating a void in the interior lines. “As soon as I found out X wasn’t going to play, a lot of things changed. He suffered a concussion and just wasn’t ready to go. Bill was out and had to piece things together on the line,” Seiden said. Piedmont looks to turn the page on the difficult night and prepares for its second Mission Division game of the season when hosting Irvington on October 17. The Vikings are currently 5-1, while PHS dominated last year’s game in a 49-7 victory. Game Recap After two trades of possession to start the first quarter, Hayward got on the board first with around 5:45 left in the quarter on a 12-yard pass to the back corner of the end zone. Piedmont contested that the reception was out of bounds, but the officials ruled the receiver in. The Farmers failed on a two-point conversion, giving them a 6-0 initial lead. But Piedmont answered on their next drive, scoring on an eight-play, 69 yard series. During the drive, Rehan Mumtaz started things with a 12-yard carry, while Dash Waters-Worthen had a 14-yard reception where he nearly broke through for a long run after the catch, but was tripped up. Berkeley Playhouse premieres the beloved musical Annie on November 7. The musical will be performed onstage through December 21. Annie is a classic Broadway musical based on the comic strip Little Orphan Annie by Harold Gray, with original music by Charles Strouse and lyrics by Martin Charnin. The show premiered in 1977 and won seven Tony Awards including Best Musical. Set during the Great Depression, it follows the optimistic orphan Annie as she escapes a harsh orphanage run by Miss Hannigan and finds a new home with billionaire Oliver Warbucks. Featuring iconic songs like “Tomorrow” and “It’s the Hard Knock Life,” Annie has become a timeless classic celebrated around the world. “This classic musical is very near and dear to my heart,” Director Megan McGrath said, adding that one of her first experiences performing was playing Tessie when she was eight years old. “I got to revisit the show again as a Boylan Sister when the Berkeley Playhouse last produced the show in 2017, and it was such a fun production to be a part of,” McGrath said. “Getting to direct and choreograph Annie at the Playhouse is a full circle moment for me, and now as a mom, I get to rediscover this story of a spirited young girl through my daughter’s eyes.” The cast includes Brendan Simon as Oliver Warbucks, Melinda Meeng as Grace Farrell, Sarah Bylsma as Miss Hannigan, Diella Wottrich as Sophie, Adam Saville as Franklin Delano Roosevelt, Milo Mee as Bert Healy, and Melody Payne Alonzo as Cecille. Cara Impallomeni will perform in Berkeley Playhouse’s production of Annie as the star character. McGrath said that despite the show taking place during the depression era, the show “positively beams with light, love, found family, and hope for a better tomorrow.” The musical is appropriate for all ages. articles.text: The Young People’s Symphony Orchestra (YPSO), the oldest independent youth orchestra in California, opens its 89th season with a fall concert on Saturday, Nov. 8, at 7:30 p.m. at First Church Berkeley. The performance features a dynamic program that includes Hector Berlioz’s Le Corsaire Overture, Maurice Ravel’s Rapsodie Espagnole, and Antonín Dvořák’s Symphony No. 8. “This concert highlights the talents of our young musicians and introduces YPSO’s new season,” said Executive Director Nadia Liu. “As we look ahead to our international tour, we are excited to share these performances with our community.” The evening opens with Berlioz’s Le Corsaire, an energetic overture known for its dramatic flair and vivid orchestration. Ravel’s Rapsodie Espagnole follows, showcasing Spanish-inspired rhythms and textures. The concert concludes with Dvořák’s Symphony No. 8, celebrated for its pastoral warmth and expressive melodies. The orchestra, composed of musicians aged 12 to 22, continues its tradition of offering professional-level performance opportunities while fostering musical education and growth. YPSO enters the new season with a focus on musical excellence and community engagement. The 2025-26 season includes a celebration of the upcoming 250th anniversary of the United States and culminates in an international tour scheduled for June 2026. Music Director David Ramadanoff has led YPSO for over three decades. He studied at the Cleveland Institute of Music and The Juilliard School, before serving as Assistant Conductor of the San Francisco Symphony. Maestro Ramadanoff chooses programs that “highlight diverse eras and composers while fostering each student’s musical growth.” Tickets for the Nov. 8 concert are available through YPSO’s website and at the door. For more information, visit ypso.org.
articles.title: YPSO opens season on Nov. 8 featuring Berlioz, Ravel and Dvořák

articles.text: Visit San Francisco’s Exploratorium every Thursday evening to experience the science museum “after hours.” After Dark is a recurring adults‑only event that transforms the museum into a late‑night playground of science, art and sensory exploration from 6 to 10 p.m. Guests aged 18 and up are invited to wander through 700+ interactive exhibits focused on science, technology, engineering and more. With the lights dimmed, guests can explore the museum’s classic galleries, a live DJ set, themed programs and alcoholic and nonalcoholic drink options at cash bars. “It’s kind of like an adult playground,” Sam Sharkland, senior program developer at the Exploratorium, told ABC7. “It’s 18+, we have cocktails available and lots of extra programming, so you can almost be a kid or scratch that scientific curiosity that you may have lost.” Each Thursday features a different theme or special programming. Previous nights have included Sexplorations, talks tied to science and culture, live performances, and temporary exhibits. On November 6, the museum will host After Dark: Soundscapes, inviting guests to explore acoustics, rhythm and vibration through the museum’s many hands‑on galleries. Tickets are required and “After Dark Membership” offers are available for frequent visitors. For more information, visit https://www.exploratorium.edu. articles.text: The San Francisco Public Library is teaming up with de Young to offer an expert-led discussion on the fine arts museum’s newest exhibition. The de Young’s Manga as Art exhibition celebrates Manga, a type of image-driven narrative storytelling in Japan. The de Young is the first North American museum to highlight in a major exhibition the contemporary Japanese art form, and features well-known artists including Chiba Tetsuya, Akatsuka Fujio, Takahashi Rumiko, Taniguchi Jiro, Yamazaki Mari, Araki Hirohiko, Yamashita Kazumi, Tagame Gengoroh, Yoshinaga Fumi, Oda Eiichiro, and Tanaami Keiichi. “Captivating millions around the world with dynamic graphic narratives, manga is one of the most significant visual mediums of our time,” said Thomas Campbell, Director and CEO of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco. “San Francisco has long been a gateway for Japanese cultural exchange in the United States, and we are delighted to honor this legacy by showcasing the artistry and power of contemporary Japanese narrative art in Art of Manga.” San Francisco State University humanities professor Hanako Asakura and manga author and anime expert Gilles Poitras will discuss the popularity boom of Japanese manga literature as well as elements of its vibrant storytelling through illustrations. The event is held at the Koret Auditorium at the Main Library in San Francisco, from 2 p.m. to 4 p.m. on Sunday, October 26. All San Francisco Public Library programs are free and open to all. For more information, visit https://sfpl.org/events. articles.text: In anticipation of the annual Artisanal Beer Festival, organizers at the Piedmont Center for the Arts have once again reached out to their community of craft brewers. Each year, they invite both returning favorites and newcomers to share their latest creations — and, of course, their inventive names. You might think that after so many festivals, the brewers would start running out of clever ideas. Not so. As in previous years, the list of names submitted for the upcoming festival proves that creativity remains one of the core ingredients in Piedmont’s brewing scene. Past festivals have featured memorable names such as Jazzman, Stub Your Toe-in-theDark Ale, Mashing Pumpkins, Cognitive Dissonance, Paul the Pilsner, Saison Du Poe, Sake to Me, and Ah, Bitter Dregs. Beyond their puns and wordplay, the brewers delight in explaining how each name ties back to the flavor and character of the beer itself. This year’s lineup promises to be just as inventive. Longtime participant Matt Gearhart will return with Rye-T-Oh! and Nothing Special Ale, while fellow veteran Aaron Bagnell will present a cream ale aptly titled Hops on Pops. Twenty-year brewer Michael Fedor will offer a pale ale brewed with hops grown right here in town — The Piedmont Pala Ave Pale. Kyle Killion has been brewing for more than fifteen years. Piedmont City Vice Mayor and 2024 judge Conna McCarthy with brewer Aaron Bagnell This year he is presenting Crimes of Passion (fruit), a Belgian Wit with passion fruit and Mr. Prickles, a prickly pear IPA. Local duo Jon and Maureen Rhodin, who have been brewing together for nine years, plan to unveil something “dank and hoppy” — though they haven’t yet settled on a name. “You know it must be good if it doesn’t even have a name yet,” joked one organizer. The festival will also feature the “People’s Choice” award, introduced last year to allow attendees to vote for their favorite beer. The inaugural winner, Trevor Fleshman, took the honor with Nipple Confusion, a single-batch American IPA inspired by his new fatherhood. New faces will also join the mix. Piedmont resident Wes Blummer, a craft brewer of four years, will make his festival debut with three beers: Grapeful Dead, a Saison titled Every Villain Is Lemons, and a Vienna lager called Big Arnold. “There’s no limit to the creativity of our brewers — in what they make or what they call it,” said festival co-organizer Carter Dunlap, who helps coordinate the event each year. Admission to this year’s festival includes a custom tasting glass and unlimited sampling for $15. An Oktoberfest-style meal of grilled bratwurst, sauerkraut and potato salad will also be available for $15. Tickets can be purchased online at tinyurl.com/ymf8mz7c or at the door via credit card or cash. For more information, contact Carter Dunlap at carter@ dunlapclan.net.

In Carrots and Counterpoint, three composers from different eras explore that question in bold, unexpected ways through the string quartet. Florence Price blends American folksongs and African spirituals with classical technique in her Five Folksongs in Counterpoint. Schubert’s Rosamunde Quartet fuses his love of song and chamber music, reworking melodies from earlier vocal pieces, including music from the play Rosamunde. It feels like a picture of America at its best — and in some ways, like the best parts of the Weimar Republic. People of all nations are everywhere and, for the most part, welcomed and appreciated. Native Germans share their country with Africans, Indians, Asians and people from across the Middle East. Schools are full, thanks to a new baby boom. Elementary education begins with first grade — there is no kindergarten — and all instruction is in German. Yet, as in America, many immigrants continue to speak their native languages at home. Singing begins in classrooms, and private music schools offer instrumental training. Youth orchestras thrive, often touring internationally. Traveling across the country, I’ve noticed that prices are much lower than in the Bay Area. Restaurant meals cost about half as much, and portions are large, even with a 19% tax. Food markets resemble those in the United States, featuring both national and regional specialties alongside international fare. Sausages — a regional dish — come in countless varieties. One of the country’s best traditions is school concerts — something I wish America would revive. Recently, I performed in a concert held in a castle for an old friend, once a leading orchestral violinist, who now lives in a fantasy world where he imagines himself the uncrowned king of Romania. Joining me was violinist and conductor Barbara Stanzeleit, a beloved local teacher, and pianist Filip Pavlov, who flew in from Bulgaria. articles.text: George MacKay in 1917 Before discussing writer/ director Sam Mendes’ film 1917, I feel I would be remiss not to mention Peter Jackson’s extraordinary They Will Not Grow Old. Jackson was given access to hundreds of archival WWI news footage from Britain’s Imperial War Museum – scratched, grainy, and hand cranked film that he, using stateof-the-art restorative technology, not only colorized but literally brought back to life. It’s as if he opened a portal in time and we see young Brits gathered on a battlefield, waiting, some, breaking the fourth wall, staring into the camera, smiling, their youthful faces filled with an optimistic eagerness that would soon be devastatingly transformed. WWI, which began in July 1914 and lasted until November 1918, was one of the deadliest wars in history. Nine million combatants and seven million civilians were killed as a direct result. Indirectly, 50 to 100 million deaths occurred worldwide, attributed to what was referred to as the “Spanish Flu,” the pandemic thought to have begun in the damp, muddy, disease-ridden trenches, conditions that were almost as lethal as the withering machinegun fire, shelling and chlorine gas faced by the troops. WWI was an extraordinary display of nationalistic hubris, bordering on a collective insanity in which millions of men, on all sides, were sacrificed for mere yards of soil. It was a nightmare of the awful, a killing field of stasis that continued beyond all reason. This is the context for Mendes’ most remarkable film, 1917, set in northern France, at the height of the war. articles.text: When I come across a film such as August Rush, released in 2009, I realize that were it not for the countless films now archived on various streaming platforms, I would have missed what proved to be a film that is immediately engaging and heartfelt throughout. Freddie Highmore portrays Evan Taylor/August Rush, an 11-year-old orphan residing in a boys’ home. He is tormented by the older boys, who consider him a “freak” because he insists he is able to hear music everywhere, even in a field of wind-swept wheat. In an early scene, Evan is asked by a social worker, Richard Jefferies (Terrance Howard), “If you could have just one thing, what would it be?” Evan looks at Richard and says, “to be found.” The story reveals that his parents — Louis Connelly (Jonathan Rhys-Meyers), an Irish band rocker, and his mother, Lyla Novacek (Keri Russell), a gifted cellist — are unaware of his existence. She was told by her self-serving father that Evan had died at birth. Believing that if he follows the music, this intangible, surreal sound, he will find his parents. articles.text: Special to the Post They say St. Andrews is a small, relatively quiet, rainy seaside town. They say the students who attend the university are some of the smartest in the United Kingdom and beyond. They say St. Andrews is a bubble, isolated from the rest of the world past the rolling green hills of the Scottish countryside and across the frigid waters of the North Sea. They say nothing has changed in the almost 700 years since the town was founded. I have found almost all of these claims to be true – except for the one about the town being quiet. Every street you travel, every pub you pass or store you enter, there is some kind of noise. Whether it’s a group of friends passionately talking on their way to a lecture, the clatter of a construction site and its crew, or the laughter of older Scottish men nursing a pint as the sun goes down. Whatever the sound, St. Andrews is filled with it in a way that makes it seem as if the air and ground are humming along. My first week at university – orientation – consisted of walking an average of 10,000 steps a day, exploring a town that for the most part still lives in the 15th century, going to a polo match on the beach, and discovering the Tesco meal deal (a genuine lifesaver in times of need). Now, after writing that sentence, I can’t believe this is my life. That the clatter of hoofbeats on the wet sand of West Sands Beach, the loud chatter of students watching the polo match unfold, and the pop of a champagne bottle could all combine into something considered normal. But even then, my attention kept turning toward the view to my right – the outline of the historic town against the gray clouds, with the sound of hoofbeats and mallet whacks to accompany it. It still feels like something straight out of a movie. As the days went on, I found that my two closest friends so far were both juniors on exchange, an Australian from Canberra and an American from Minnesota. I met the Minnesotan while I was lost and desperately trying to find IT, and with true Midwestern hospitality she immediately helped me. We parted ways, but later that night at a dorm bonding event I saw her again and she introduced me to the girl from Australia. The three of us live on the same floor, so most nights, when we aren’t drowning in assignments and readings, we’re in one of our rooms watching a show in the background while we talk about everything and anything. And while I’m acutely aware that both of them will be leaving after the first semester, that’s a problem for me to handle in December. Not to worry, I have plenty of other friends: a Scot and an Italian I walk with every Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday morning to our International Relations class. We once got into quite a debate about driving licenses and the legitimacy of an American one, because apparently it’s too easy to be considered a test. I was offended, but they weren’t entirely wrong. I have a German friend to get coffee with, another Australian to play tennis with, a Brit to discuss shows we’ve both watched and their insanely bad plot points. Too many nationalities, but that is the point: St. Andrews is truly international. When classes started, I found it surreal to walk through buildings and quads that are centuries old. As an American, our history mostly dates to 1776. While that’s a decent chunk of time, it’s nothing like living in the first dorm ever built at St. Andrews and walking down the same hallways people 200 years ago walked down. Or even studying in a library whose floor creaks with every step because the wood is older than everyone there combined. It’s strange that in Scotland, this kind of history is so… normal. That’s honestly the only way I can put it. In the same breath you can look at a Pret a Manger and see the remains of what once was Scotland’s oldest and largest abbey before it was destroyed by Henry the Eighth. Since being here, I’ve taken a day trip to Edinburgh, started exploring local pubs with friends, snuck into the postgraduate library because it’s built in a church (the stained glass sets the mood for reading history), and helped a friend beachcomb for seashells for a biology class. Every day seems to bring something new – running through the rain back to my dorm after medieval history, helping a friend hunt down her stolen package, sitting by the sea with takeaway fish and chips. The possibilities feel endless. They say the rain is an inconvenience. They say the cigarette butts between the cobblestones are just garbage. They say the smell of the old buildings isn’t pleasant. But I say the rain blurs the edges of reality, shrouding St. Andrews in mystery. I say the cigarette butts unite the students and locals. I say the smell of the old buildings is a reminder of the generations of students who came before us. St. Andrews is more than it seems. It’s not just a town that houses the oldest university in Scotland. It’s a town for anyone to enjoy whether playing a round of golf with the North Sea to your right, wandering through narrow alleyways, or sitting in a coffee shop with a cup of tea while storm clouds roll in. It doesn’t matter who you are or what you like; St. Andrews may be small, but it has a bit of everything. Larissa Edel is a Piedmont resident and former Post intern who is now a first-year student at the University of St. Andrews in Scotland. St. Andrews University in Fife, Scotland

articles.text: An increasing number of couples are choosing to include their furry friends in their wedding day, and it’s easy to see why! Your dog is a beloved member of the family, and having them by your side on your special day can make it even more unforgettable. However, incorporating your pup can add an extra layer of chaos to an already stressful event. Luckily, with some careful planning and simple tips, you can include your pawsome partner in your wedding day stress-free. First, be sure to plan your schedule carefully for the days leading up to the ceremony. Does your dog need a grooming appointment? Schedule it with enough time for touch-ups. Also make sure it is close enough to the big day that you can ensure your pooch remains perfectly coiffed. If you’re purchasing accessories like a custom flower girl collar or ring bearer pillow to attach to your pup’s harness, make sure to order items way ahead of time and do a dress rehearsal to avoid last-minute issues. If your dog is joining you at a destination wedding, make sure to pack their essentials including food, medication, waste bags, and a crate. The crate will provide a safe space for your dog to decompress during the festivities, ensuring Fluffy is alert and smiling in her photos. One of the most important things to plan for is assigning someone the role of designated dog attendant. This is one more way to greatly reduce stress on your wedding day. This person will be in charge of holding your fur baby during the ceremony, bringing them to photos, and caring for them during the reception. Finally, if you’re incorporating your dog into the ceremony, make extra time to rehearse in order to teach your dog where to go, and who to go to. Make sure someone at either end of the aisle has a leash handy. And remember, if your dog doesn’t behave exactly as planned on the wedding day, this often makes for a memorable and hilarious moment rather than an embarrassing one. can ensure a stress-free and enjoyable wedding day experience for both you and your furry friend. Remember, your wedding day is about celebrating your love, and with a little planning, your dog can be a happy and integral part of it. articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment’s Walking on Wednesdays group enjoyed a special walk last week led by walker and architect Jim Kellogg. The outing, titled Piedmont Heritage Trees and Architectural Heritage, combined a tour of the city’s distinctive trees with a look at how Piedmont’s architectural character first took shape in the late 19th century. pages.text: Wednesday, October 15, 2025 21 Walking on Wednesday Walking on Wednesdays explores Piedmont’s heritage trees and architecture By Jim Kellogg The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment’s Walking on Wednesdays group enjoyed a special walk last week led by walker and architect Jim Kellogg. The outing, titled Piedmont Heritage Trees and Architectural Heritage, combined a tour of the city’s distinctive trees with a look at how Piedmont’s architectural character first took shape in the late 19th century. A strong turnout of about 40 walkers and three canine companions gathered at the Exedra on a crisp fall morning. From there, the group followed a loop that took them past City Hall, along Bonita Avenue and Park Way to Dracena Park, and back to the Recreation Department Building by way of Jerome and Magnolia Avenues. Along the route, walkers learned about the origins of Piedmont’s architectural styles, the city’s Heritage Tree program, and even received a preview of the soon-to-open Piedmont Community Pool. Kellogg began by describing the Piedmont Heritage Tree program, launched in 2018 and coordinated by parks and project manager Nancy Kent. The program’s goal is to recognize distinctive trees notable for their size, species, location, or historical importance in Piedmont’s parks and open spaces. Since its inception, the Park Commission has designated 28 Heritage Trees. A full list, with photos and an interactive map, can be found at piedmont.ca.gov. Just steps from the Exedra are six examples of these designated trees. They include the Highland Poplar grove encircling the Exedra itself, two majestic Coast Live Oaks, the tall Coastal Redwood used for Piedmont’s holiday tree lighting, the Yulan Magnolia gracing the front of Community Hall, and the Akebono Cherry grove that surrounds the Japanese Tea House in Piedmont Park. From there, Kellogg guided the walkers to Vista Avenue, where two “Mountain Moon” evergreen magnolias stand prominently in front of City Hall. The group then paused at the Wetmore House on Vista and Bonita Avenues, built in 1878. Kellogg explained that the home, the oldest in Piedmont, is an excellent example of French Colonial–Plantation style architecture. Across the street, City Hall, designed in 1910 by architect Albert Farr, represents the Spanish Mission Revival style that would influence many of Piedmont’s later civic buildings, including Frank C. Havens Elementary School. Continuing down Bonita Avenue, walkers viewed several homes that capture the transition between architectural eras. The Bekenfeld House at 227 Bonita, built in 1895, remains Piedmont’s finest Queen Anne Victorian, complete with spindle detailing and a whimsical carved gargoyle in its front gable. Next door, the Esty House at 231 Bonita, built just a year later, reflects an entirely different vision—a shingle-sided Berkeley Craftsman with multiple gables, dormers, and handcrafted redwood interiors. As Kellogg noted, Piedmont’s style shifted quickly at the turn of the century from ornate Victorian to the simpler, nature-inspired Craftsman aesthetic. Another highlight was the Harold Farr House at 127 Bonita, built in 1907. Designed by Albert Farr for his brother, it was the architect’s first project in Piedmont and showcases his early Craftsman design with a cedar shingle exterior and multiple gabled roofs. Farr’s later works, like City Hall, revealed his adaptability as he embraced the Mission Revival look that became his hallmark. The group continued down Park Way to Dracena Park, where they encountered four more Heritage Trees. These included a mature Coastal Live Oak, a California Buckeye recently nominated for Heritage status by residents Jack and Sharona Fischrup, a native Bigleaf Maple, and a grove of six Dawn Redwoods in the old quarry area. Kellogg shared that Dawn Redwoods were once thought extinct—known only from fossils—until living specimens were rediscovered in central China in 1948. Today they are thriving again and stand as one of only three remaining redwood species alongside the Coastal Redwood and the Giant Sequoia. From Dracena Park, the walkers proceeded along Latham Street to Jerome and Fairview Avenues, where they viewed a contemporary remodeled home showcasing modernist, sustainable design. With horizontal redwood siding and brightly colored stucco accents, the home draws inspiration from Mexican architect Luis Barragán, whose modernist approach celebrated color, light, and simplicity. Kellogg noted that several new Piedmont homes now feature modernist or sustainable elements, representing a broader interpretation of architectural heritage than the city’s early-20th-century roots. The tour concluded at the Piedmont Community Pool complex, where Hadley Clegg, the Recreation Department’s aquatic coordinator, greeted the group. Clegg described the nearly completed facility, now in its commissioning phase, which will soon open for community use. The complex includes a 27-meter, 12-lane competition pool; a large multi-depth family pool; locker and restroom facilities; a multipurpose community room for small events; and an outdoor rooftop pavilion with panoramic views of the grounds. Both pools will feature year-round heated water, and programs will include swim training, lap swimming, water polo, and rental options for group activities. The walkers were impressed by the design and the promise of expanded recreation opportunities for residents. “It’s wonderful to see how the city is blending heritage with the future,” one participant remarked. The Walking on Wednesdays group continues to meet each week at 10:30 a.m. at the Exedra, at the corner of Highland and Magnolia Avenues. Everyone is welcome to join, including friendly dogs. There is no cost to participate, though registration is required. To register, visit tinyurl.com/3ethkehu or call (510) 420-3070 for more information.
